clinicalPearls: The three overarching goals of diabetes care are to relieve hyperglycemic symptoms, reduce or prevent long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications, and allow as normal a lifestyle as possible; symptoms usually resolve once plasma glucose is below ~200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L), so therapy mainly targets complication prevention. (Harrison 22e p.3205)

HbA1c reflects average glycemia over the prior 2-3 months because erythrocytes live ~120 days, with the most recent month contributing roughly half the value; it does not capture short-term variability or recent intercurrent illness the way continuous (CGM) or fingerstick (BGM) monitoring does. (Harrison 22e p.3207-3208)

Continuous glucose monitoring measures interstitial glucose, which is in equilibrium with blood glucose but can lag when glucose changes rapidly or during exercise; an ambulatory glucose profile summarizes time-in-range, time above/below target, the glucose management indicator (correlating with HbA1c), and glucose variability. (Harrison 22e p.3207)

The general HbA1c goal is below 7% (or <=6.5% for selected patients), but a more lenient target of <7.5-8% is appropriate for those with cognitive impairment, hypoglycemia unawareness, or limited life expectancy; about one in four people over 65 has diabetes, so elderly targets must be individualized. (Harrison 22e p.3208)

A consensus CGM time-in-range goal for most patients with type 1 or type 2 DM is >70% of time within 70-180 mg/dL (3.9-10.0 mmol/L), with <4% below 70 mg/dL and <1% below 54 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3208)

Ketones (preferably blood beta-hydroxybutyrate rather than urine nitroprusside assays, which detect only acetoacetate and acetone) should be checked in type 1 DM whenever plasma glucose persistently exceeds 250 mg/dL (13.9 mmol/L) or during intercurrent illness with nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain. (Harrison 22e p.3216)
DKA arises mostly in type 1 DM and HHS mostly in type 2 DM, but the two exist along a continuum of hyperglycemia and up to one-third of patients show features of both. (Harrison 22e p.3216)

Ketosis-prone diabetes can present with DKA at diagnosis in obese young adults of Hispanic or African descent who later recover insulin secretory capacity and can discontinue insulin after weeks to months. (Harrison 22e p.3216)

SGLT-2 inhibitor therapy can precipitate euglycemic DKA in type 2 DM, where glucose is normal or only mildly elevated because of glucosuria, so a normal glucose does not exclude ketoacidosis; resolution should be tracked by bicarbonate correction rather than by glucose. (Harrison 22e p.3216-3217)

In DKA the measured serum sodium is artifactually low; the correction adds ~1.6 mmol/L of sodium for each 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) rise in glucose, and a normal measured sodium in DKA signals a profound free-water deficit. (Harrison 22e p.3217)

Inpatient hyperglycemia predicts worse outcomes, yet very strict glycemic control in the critically ill worsens outcomes; the NICE-SUGAR trial showed higher mortality and more severe hypoglycemia with a target of 81-108 mg/dL versus a moderate goal of <180 mg/dL, supporting a hospital target of roughly 140-180 mg/dL. (Harrison 22e p.3219)

Sliding-scale insulin alone (reactive treatment only when glucose is already high) is inadequate for inpatient management; scheduled basal plus prandial and corrective dosing is preferred, and CGM/automated insulin delivery are not FDA approved for ICU use. (Harrison 22e p.3219-3220)
harrison.pathophysiology: Hyperglycemia in diabetes reflects relative or absolute insulin deficiency with impaired glucose utilization and unrestrained hepatic glucose production. In acute decompensation, severe hyperglycemia drives osmotic diuresis with volume depletion. DKA results from relative or absolute insulin deficiency combined with excess counterregulatory hormones (glucagon, catecholamines, cortisol, growth hormone); the low insulin-to-glucagon ratio promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, and ketone body formation, while increased lipolysis releases free fatty acids that are shifted toward ketogenesis, producing ketonemia and high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated in both DKA and HHS. HHS is caused by relative (less severe) insulin deficiency plus inadequate fluid intake; insulin deficiency raises hepatic glucose output and impairs muscle uptake, and osmotic diuresis with poor fluid replacement produces extreme hyperglycemia, hyperosmolality, and dehydration. The absence of significant ketosis in HHS is incompletely understood but is attributed to only partial insulin deficiency, lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels, and an insulin/glucagon balance that does not favor ketogenesis. During exercise or acute illness, surges in counterregulatory hormones and cytokines cause transient insulin resistance and can tip toward hyperglycemia or, with relative hyperinsulinemia, hypoglycemia.
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
Acute pancreatitis or surgical abdomen (DKA abdominal pain can mimic these; hyperamylasemia in DKA is usually salivary, so serum lipase is needed)
Lactic acidosis (a small anion-gap acidosis from lactate can accompany HHS)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute pancreatitis / acute surgical abdomen presenting with abdominal pain mimicking DKA
Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses (starvation, alcohol, toxins)
Alternative causes of altered mental status or coma (stroke, hypoxemia, intoxication) overlapping with severe DKA/HHS presentation
additionalInvestigations: HbA1c at initial evaluation and at least twice yearly when at goal, every 3 months when control is inadequate or therapy changed (interpret with caution in hemoglobinopathies, anemias, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, G6PD variants, hemodialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy)
Continuous glucose monitoring or capillary blood glucose monitoring for short-term control and time-in-range
Blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (preferred over urine nitroprusside ketone assays)
Serum electrolytes with anion gap, potassium, phosphate and magnesium (every 4 h in early DKA), bicarbonate, arterial pH
Serum/plasma glucose every 1-2 h during acute crises
BUN and creatinine (intravascular volume depletion / prerenal azotemia), serum osmolality
Serum lipase if pancreatitis suspected (amylase in DKA is often salivary and nondiagnostic)
Workup for precipitant: cultures, chest x-ray, ECG; corrected sodium calculation
Fructosamine or glycated albumin as alternative measures reflecting glycemia over the prior 2-4 weeks
redFlags: Nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain in a person with type 1 DM (warrants immediate evaluation for DKA)
Kussmaul respirations and a fruity (acetone) breath odor
Lethargy progressing to obtundation or coma; cerebral edema (especially in children during DKA resolution)
Hypotension and tachycardia from volume depletion
Plasma glucose persistently >250 mg/dL or, in HHS, markedly elevated (>1000 mg/dL) with hyperosmolality (>300 mOsm)
Normal measured serum sodium during DKA (indicates profound water deficit)
Hypoglycemia, particularly recurrent, nocturnal, or with hypoglycemia unawareness
Signs of a precipitating event (infection, myocardial infarction, stroke, pancreatitis) even without fever
harrison.prognosis: With appropriate therapy, DKA mortality is low (<1%) and relates more to the underlying or precipitating event (infection/pneumonia, COVID-19, pregnancy, end-stage renal disease, myocardial infarction) than to the metabolic derangement itself; venous thrombosis, upper GI bleeding, ARDS, and cerebral edema (chiefly in children, during resolution) can complicate the course. Even a single DKA episode carries a substantially increased 1-year mortality, and recurrent DKA may signal underlying mental health issues or barriers to care such as insulin cost. HHS carries a substantially higher mortality (up to ~15% in some series) because patients are typically older with serious precipitating illness and comorbidities. Improved glycemic control reduces microvascular complications regardless of baseline level, and early intensive control in type 1 DM (DCCT/EDIC) lowered later cardiovascular events nearly two decades on.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal or only mildly elevated glucose excludes ketoacidosis; euglycemic DKA occurs with SGLT-2 inhibitors and resolution must be judged by bicarbonate, not glucose
Relying on urine nitroprusside ketone tests, which miss beta-hydroxybutyrate (the dominant ketone) and give false positives with captopril, penicillamine, or valproic acid
Interpreting hyperamylasemia in DKA as pancreatitis when it is usually salivary in origin; obtain lipase
Failing to correct serum sodium for hyperglycemia, masking a true free-water deficit
Misreading the early/at-presentation serum potassium as adequate; total-body potassium is depleted despite a normal or high initial level, and hypokalemia develops during insulin/fluid therapy
Trusting HbA1c in conditions that alter red-cell turnover (hemoglobinopathy, anemia, reticulocytosis, transfusion, uremia, dialysis, erythropoietin or HIV therapy)
Using sliding-scale insulin alone for inpatients, which is inadequate
Applying overly strict inpatient glucose targets, which increases severe hypoglycemia and can worsen outcomes (NICE-SUGAR)
Substances interfering with glucose sensors/meters (e.g., acetaminophen, ascorbic acid, hydroxyurea, mannitol/sorbitol for CGM; uric acid, galactose, xylose, L-DOPA for BGM)
harrison.severityClassification: DKA severity is graded by pH, serum bicarbonate, and mental status: mild (pH 7.25-7.30, bicarbonate 15-18 meq/L, normal mentation); moderate (pH 7.0-7.25, bicarbonate 10-15 meq/L, mildly reduced mentation); severe (pH <7.0, bicarbonate <10-15 meq/L, reduced mental status or coma). Representative presenting laboratory ranges: DKA glucose ~250-600 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 meq/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0 mmol/L, and elevated anion gap; HHS glucose ~600-1200 mg/dL (may exceed 1000) with osmolality >300, bicarbonate >18, pH >7.3, and absent/minimal ketones; euglycemic DKA glucose ~100-250 mg/dL with bicarbonate <18 and beta-hydroxybutyrate >3.0.
management: Set individualised glycaemic goals guided by HbA1c, more lenient with frailty, hypoglycaemia unawareness or limited life expectancy, and targeting time-in-range
Type 2 pharmacotherapy stepped from metformin with addition of SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists for cardiorenal benefit; type 1 requires basal-bolus insulin or pump therapy
Continuous or capillary glucose monitoring with structured self-management education
Diabetic ketoacidosis: intravenous fluid resuscitation, an insulin infusion and careful potassium replacement, with treatment of the precipitant
Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: aggressive fluid replacement, insulin and electrolyte correction with attention to thromboprophylaxis
Check blood beta-hydroxybutyrate ketones during intercurrent illness or persistent hyperglycaemia in type 1 diabetes
Surveillance for and prevention of long-term microvascular and macrovascular complications
Multidisciplinary care with escalation to critical care for severe metabolic decompensation
